title: Music and Nations
objective: After this level you can explain how composers used folk music to express national identity.
summary: Romantic nationalism drew on folk tunes, dances and legends: Smetana's Vltava paints a Czech river; Sibelius's Finlandia hid from Russian censors.

cards.headline: A piece of music once had to travel under a fake name.
cards.body: In 1899, one orchestral piece, with no words at all, made the censors of an empire nervous. It was sometimes billed under harmless titles so it could be played at all. Why would anyone fear a tune? Because in the Romantic era, music had become a way of saying who you were.

cards.headline: Sounding like home
cards.body: Britannica describes musical nationalism as a nation's distinctive features revealed and glorified in music, and it played a big part in the Romantic era. Composers drew on folk tunes, folk dances, folklore and village life. Leaders included Glinka in Russia, Smetana and Dvořák for Czech music, and Grieg in Norway. You've already met one example: Chopin's mazurkas in Level 44.

cards.headline: A river as a national portrait
cards.body: Bedřich Smetana's Vltava (The Moldau) follows the river from its source in the Bohemian Forest, past hunters and a village wedding in polka rhythm, all the way to Prague. It's the second of six parts of Má vlast, 'My Country'. And here's the echo of Level 42: Smetana became totally deaf in late 1874, and he wrote Má vlast between then and 1879.

cards.headline: Finlandia in disguise
cards.body: In 1899 Finland was under tsarist Russia, and its press was censored. Jean Sibelius wrote Finlandia for a celebration that was really a rally for a free press. To slip past Russian censors, early performances sometimes used titles like 'Impromptu' or 'Happy Feelings at the Awakening of Finnish Spring'. Nobody could arrest a spring.

questions.prompt: What did Romantic nationalist composers draw on to make music sound like their nation?

options.label: Ancient Greek theory and plainchant
options.rationale: They looked to their own folk traditions.

options.label: Folk tunes, folk dances and folklore
Imported Italian opera tunes
options.rationale: The point was to sound distinctly national.

options.label: Random notes chosen by dice
options.rationale: Nationalism drew on shared folk traditions.

questions.explanation: Nationalist composers drew on folk tunes and dances, folklore and village life to reveal their nation's character.

questions.prompt: Why was Sibelius's Finlandia sometimes performed under names like 'Impromptu'?

options.label: Sibelius couldn't decide on a title
The orchestra had lost the original score
options.rationale: The music was the same; only the name hid it.

options.label: To enter it in a piano competition
options.rationale: It's an orchestral piece with a political purpose.

questions.explanation: Written for a veiled rally for press freedom under tsarist Russia, it sometimes used neutral titles to avoid censorship.

questions.prompt: Like Beethoven in Level 42, Smetana composed after losing his hearing. What did he write once totally deaf?
questions.explanation: Smetana went totally deaf in late 1874 and wrote the six parts of Má vlast between then and 1879.
